utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My apologies for having kept everybody waiting. Sir, could I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, good afternoon. I would just like to remind you yesterday at the start of my cross-examination, I would like to ask you after I put my question, that you wait a little bit before you start answering so that the interpreters can complete their interpretation of the question. Thank you. Yesterday you mentioned the nature of your contacts with Mr. Marin Vidic. We've heard from Mrs. Bosanac here that Marin Vidic, shortly before the fall of Vukovar, intended to talk to Mr. Goran Hadzic, and I think that this was also the topic of a government meeting of the Republic of Croatia on the 11th of November, 1991. Did you know anything about the intention of Mr. Vidic to speak to Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first time that I'm hearing of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you mentioned members of the Vukovar Territorial Defence. Did you know a person by the name of Stanko Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps I knew him just superficially.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Milan Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a question which Vujovic. There are many Vujovics in Vukovar. We clarified this in Belgrade that that wasn't the person that I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Dusan Jaksic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. Could you please tell me if you remember that at one point the JNA barracks in Vukovar was blockaded and it was supposed to surrender to the Croatian defence forces. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The soldiers apparently flew the white flag and then when the soldiers were supposed to -- when they were on the point of entering the barracks, the flag had disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what time of the year it was, if you are unable to remember the exact day?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was perhaps in mid-November or maybe a little bit earlier. I cannot remember the exact day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're talking about 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that from September 1991 there was the staff and logistics of the Serb Territorial Defence at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we all knew that something was going on, even where it was going on. It obviously was happening at Velepromet because we could observe the consequences of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yesterday we talked about how you got to the hospital and also about the time that you spent there. What I would like to know is if you remember when you boarded the bus going from the hospital to the barracks. Do you remember seeing people wearing hospital uniforms or white coats or jackets but who were not hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean inside the hospital or in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really pay any attention to that. I was just thinking about the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see people dressed like this in the bus, the bus that you boarded once you left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can I just remind you that in the conversation you had with the Canadian lieutenant-colonel, Ms. Kim Carter, you said that these people were in the buses and that you even advised them that they should take off these coats? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you had put the question like that, I would have replied, yes. These were people who were supposed to go to the same place that I was going to, but they had put on white coats in order to possibly protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cakalic. Do you know a person by the name of Zdenko Novak?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know him from before these events or did you meet him during these events in 1991 in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we all knew each other by sight, we knew each other by nicknames or first name or our last name. I learnt a lot about Zdenko Novak when he was taken to Belgrade when his father made great efforts to save him. And it wasn't just his father, it was others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I mentioned the buses that took you to the barracks from the hospital. Am I right when I say that these were Cazmatrans buses, the company from Vukovar with Vukovar registration plates?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that these were Vukovar buses, but the young men told me that these were not Vukovar buses, so I believed them. I don't always have to be right. Don't ask me about the colour either. I don't recall the colour at all now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about the colour, of course. But I will ask you the following: In 1993 in this interview you had with the Canadian army lieutenant-colonel said that these were Cazmatrans buses with Vukovar licence plates?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I thought that these were our buses, our buses from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point the soldiers who were searching you as you were leaving the hospital said that you were supposed to be exchanged for officers, soldiers and their families who were in the territory of Croatia in the hands of the Croatian armed forces. Not you personally but you as a group.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember. The thinking was that we were all going to be saved together. This is what we were aiming for, what we were thinking of, but this didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not going to deal with the barracks and the hospital anymore. My colleagues will deal with that, because we're trying to save time. What I will ask you is it the following: What time did you leave the barracks to go to Ovcara? Did you look at a watch or can you tell us approximately what time it was?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime after 2.00. We arrived at Ovcara at around 2.30, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you look at a watch or is this just an assessment?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I mean, you know that everything that we were going through, that whole process was quite difficult and painful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you described how you disembarked from the buses at Ovcara, and you told us that the buses in front of you emptied first and then the next bus would come and so on. Is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The buses stopped in front of the hangar, maybe 10 or 15 metres away. In Belgrade three lawyers asked me about that, one after the other, and then finally I said it was between 10 and 30 metres. Don't hold me to my word. I wasn't sure what the distance was, but the next time, as soon as I get to Vukovar, I'm going to measure the exact distance. I'm sorry, you put a question to me but I was talking about something else. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No problem at all. What I asked was that the bus that was emptied, would it leave and then be replaced by the next bus so that people could disembark from that bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The place where people were getting off the buses would be where one bus after another unloaded its passengers. Once that bus left the next bus would come, the second, the third bus, and finally the fifth bus. I don't know where they turned around. I mean do you know how we were running into the hangar? We kept our heads down, we needed to protect our heads. It didn't even occur to me to think about where the buses were turning around and where they were going after.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you that. I'm not going ask you about where they turned around. All I was asking you is how they were moving in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how they moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you talked about the gauntlet in front of the hangar that you had to run through on your way out of the bus. Can you remember how far the gauntlet was from the bus that would stop to unload its passengers? You don't have to give us the exact distance. Approximately.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, more than a metre and a half away for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me if you can tell how long was the gauntlet? Did it reach the hangar itself or did it stop short before the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked the same question in Belgrade, and I said that the next time I go I'm going to please get your address and then I can let you know exactly how far it was from the entrance of the hangar. I don't know. I mean, I think that as soon as -- I already showed you under which conditions we were entering the hangar. This was an unpleasant event that I'm trying to forget as much as possible, so it's not so easy for me every time to recall these painful memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I am in the position to contribute to your discomfort, but I do have to ask you anything that I believe would be of importance for these proceedings. Of course I don't need to know precisely how long the gauntlet was. What I'm interested in is how much distance did you have to cover before you reached the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably around 10 metres, something like that. I said probably. I didn't really give you the exact timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw Slavko Dokmanovic standing in front in an air force lieutenant-colonel's blue uniform. Did you think that he was an officer, since you knew that he was the president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I said that he was -- did I say that he was wearing the uniform of an air force soldier?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that he was wearing a blue uniform?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't say anything about an air force soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you said he was wearing a blue uniform of a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he had a Tito-style cap on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yesterday you told us how they broke your glasses when you descended from the bus, but you didn't tell us what strength glasses you had, what was the prescription of your glasses at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say that yesterday, but I can -- I have it here. I can tell you now. Just a little bit of patience, please. I don't think I have it with me. I didn't bring it with me. Ah, here it is. I've found it. The right eye plus 3.00, and the other eye is plus 2.75. Actually, that's both the right eye, and the left eye is plus 3.25, and plus 3.00. And then you know that you actually to get the right figure you add the two figures together. I always find it very difficult to remember that. I mean it is my -- they are my glasses, but I just never seem to remember the exact strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting my learned friend. I know he asked the question for the prescription at the time, but I've seen the -- the translation. And I wonder perhaps if he could just clarify if that is actually the prescription then as opposed to now, so there is no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I'm going to do that, if this is something that my learned friend would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I was asking you about the prescription of your glasses at the time. Did you give us the strength at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the situation right now, and it always changes, it varies. And I did feel a worsening, a difference recently, so I did go to check my eyes again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But can you tell us what your prescription for your glasses was then in November, 1991, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I should know that, but I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At the time was your prescription plus or minus; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the same as it is now, but only less.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember telling the Canadian lieutenant-colonel that your prescription at the time for one eye was 2.15 and the other one was 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, interpreter's correction, 3.95.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is possible. I responded to all sorts of questions, so I could have responded to that one as well. Perhaps I recall that at the time. Well, they broke my glasses, I've already told you about that, and I was without them for all of that time. When I returned to Croatia, I went to have my eyes tested then, and then it was important to get the right prescription.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you wear glasses only for certain types of activity or all the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wore them all the time. All the time. I don't know exactly since when.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just to make this perfectly clear and to give you a chance to remind yourself of what you said, I'll read out a portion of the transcript. This is your interview with lieutenant-colonel --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a lady, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, Kim Carter. The date is the 6th of March, 1993. For the benefit of my learned friends, the page is 00596187. The translator: "Can you tell us what your prescription is for your glasses, how near-sighted are you and are you able to see without your glasses?" Your answer: "2.15 for what's up close and 3.95 for reading."

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was my answer, then it should be correct, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've got a different reading on my -- my translation. If it's page 6187, the English translation that I have is 2.15, and then for looking at distance, and then 3.5 for reading. That's what I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're quite right. That's what I read out. At least I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So in the two places where you mentioned 3.95 it should be 3.5. Is that correct, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It says 3.95. Oh, right, my apologies. I've just looked at the English. In the Croatian copy it says 3.95 and in the English it says 3.05.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I try to say something about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I just told you, my right eye now is 3.00, and 2.75. That's my present prescription for my right eye. For my left eye, it's 3.25 over plus 3. This was made on the 12th of December, the new prescription, because I knew you'd ask and I didn't really know it by heart, what the index was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've shared this with us, and I think this is now beyond dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, am I expected to further clarify this or may I just move on with my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, I bid you to move on, Mr. Vasic, reminding you that you almost have spent three quarters of the time that the Prosecutor spent examining on your own cross-examination. That gives your learned colleagues very limited scope of time. So I think they would urge you, along with the Chamber, to get to matters that are important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. I have less than 10 questions to go; therefore, it shouldn't take too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, while you were inside the hangar you did not see any pieces of machinery there? You said so to the lieutenant-colonel, the Canadian lady, as well as at the Dokmanovic trial here in The Hague, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I said so, then that must be right. But there's something else I have to tell you. On our way into the hangar, there were those two men leaning against the wall with their legs spread and their hands pressed against the wall. On our way in we saw this, and there were stacks of hay inside. That was another thing we saw. There was plenty of that and that's where we sat down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were then taken outside the hangar. What I want to know is, roughly speaking, what time it might have been, if you can say?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was still natural light, if that's what you mean, outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please have ERN 00531231 shown, page 22? Just briefly, please. This is the photograph of the hangar that my learned friends showed you yesterday. And if the usher could please just hand the witness a pen so that you can mark for us the exact spot where you were standing when you had just been taken outside the hangar and before you reached that vehicle that was later to drive you to Velepromet. Thank you. Should I repeat the number for you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll describe that for you, if there is no way you can track it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, for the sake of saving some time, maybe that would be our best shot at it. It would be simpler and quicker, too, if you could just point it out for us. But meanwhile, please try to describe how far that was from the hangar door and to which side?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please try to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where were you exactly when you were taken outside the hangar waiting for the vehicle that eventually drove you to Velepromet to fetch you, to pick you up?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that the hangar walls were made of tin and they had sliding doors. Have you ever been at Ovcara yourself? Because that might help me give you a better idea.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel's answer inaudible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that when you approached the hangar there's a rather large building there perhaps 200 metres long and there was a well there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But here is the photograph and it might be easier to do it like this. Just zoom in slightly, please, the area where the hangar is. Sir, is this large enough for you to mark the spot for us?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is three different hangars you're showing me now, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I mean the one that you were in. Zoom in a little more, please. That might help the witness see clearer. Do you now recognise the hangar in which you were?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a hard copy. I don't know if that will help in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly my picture is very poor, as normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, is this photograph clear enough for you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are other hangars that I can see. Right behind there is the oblong one partly obscured by trees and three other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But do you recognise the one in which you were?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be the one that is in front of those other two, the one to the right. Because this is where the large door is. There's one window to the right, and then several windows on the other side. Then there's a tree and the exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark the spot where you were standing once you were outside the hangar waiting for that vehicle to take you to Velepromet, if you could use a cross, please, or --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little cross right here. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is a letter A, right? So that was the spot where you came out and waited for the vehicle. You remained in that spot until the vehicle arrived?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we never went far from this spot. We were there all the time and we were speaking to those TO people that we knew and also to the man who eventually saved my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek that this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit 267.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, you said yesterday that you left Ovcara at dusk. Do you remember that on the 6th of March, 1993 you stated to the Canadian lieutenant-colonel that it was passed 6.00 p.m. when you left Ovcara, you couldn't say exactly, but it was already dark. That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But even at half past 5.00 in the afternoon it's already dark that time of the year. But if that's what it says, then I must have said it and I stand by that. I have warned you about this already, please bear this in mind. We talking about the time-line, I tried to be not very specific because I simply can't say. I usually say it was around this time or around that time, and I see that you are just holding me to it all the time, which shouldn't be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cakalic, that's precisely what I said. I quoted you as saying that you couldn't say exactly, but I'll just read out the relevant portion to see what exactly it was hat you said. The translator: "Can you remember, at least in very rough terms, what the time was when you and the other six men left Ovcara?" My apologies. For my learned friends, this is 00596178 and 00596179. And your answer was: "Sometime past 6.00. I can't say exactly. It was dark already."

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you remember how long it took you to get from Ovcara to Velepromet, roughly speaking of course?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance must be five or six kilometres. Half an hour at the very most. I'm doing this deliberately and this is just a speculation or an estimate. And may that be recorded, please. It's an estimate on my part, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again. The translation that I have is different from the translation that's coming across on the LiveNote. What I have is: "It could have been after 6.00 p.m., but I can't tell you precisely." And that's the translation that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's precisely what I said to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the Croatian language, which I suppose was the original language of your statement, and the language you used in the interview, the substance is the same. "Sometime past 6.00. I can't say exactly. It was dark already." I don't see there's really that much difference from what my learned friend is suggesting. Thank you. When you reached Velepromet you said that there was a person there whom you knew well, because he took some exams with you. He was one of the persons in charge of Velepromet and he did not -- was he in charge of Velepromet when you came there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were brought to Velepromet under escort. There were armed soldiers escorting us, and they were to leave us there. There was this one lad who was on duty who said, "I'll call the commander now." It was then that I saw him. I think he was a sales assistant somewhere in Negoslavci and he had taken one of his exams with me. But that's got nothing to do with this. I'm trying to say something else. Those soldiers who had brought us, not the one who was driving, said this: "Here you have the worst criminals from Vukovar and we are turning them over to you. You keep watchful eye on these. If we're not here by 7.00 tomorrow morning, you have to kill them."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that yesterday, but what I want to know is this person who came and who was supposed to decide whether they will take you in or not, this person's last name, can it possibly be Bingulac? Just wanted to check if you knew that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Throughout your stay in Sremska Mitrovica, were you at any point questioned by anyone from the Eastern Slavonia and Srem government?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're skipping a huge chunk of my story there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, my other friends and other Defence teams will be asking you about that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was interviewed, and I was met by Hadzic in Sremska Mitrovica. It was a Saturday, and there were no JNA officers around at that time, which is an important point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you meet anyone else from the government from the Eastern Slavonia and Srem government there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Borislavic. He kept saying it's not true that I saw him, but I did. He was a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me something else, sir. In Sremska Mitrovica were you questioned by a security officer, perhaps someone by the name of Bogdan Vujic, also known as Colonel Branko? It was a code-name that he was using at the time.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Branko, Colonel Branko. Yes, there was a man called Colonel Branko who questioned me at least about 10 times. I can tell you what he looked like, but I'm not sure if that's the name. Quite tall, a colonel by rank. He had greying, wavy hair. And he was quite an all right person to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In late February 1991, you were exchanged for a JNA colonel, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To wrap up my cross-examination, I would like to play you a brief clip. The 65 ter number is video 31 V0001260.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we didn't freeze the frame in the best possible place. Can we try again, please? What I'm interested in is this person on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this person on the right side?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The Defence claims that this was taped on the 20th of November, 1991. Do you still abide by your statement that he was at Ovcara in a blue uniform with lieutenant-colonel insignia?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also on the day that I mentioned before that was when we were beaten severely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, thank you very much for all your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like this to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Cakalic, you said that Dokmanovic was on the right side. Do you mean the man who is in the reddish or brown jacket or the man with the moustache who is shorter, to the right of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, he is on his left side, but on the right side as I am looking at the image. Dokmanovic is the person with the moustache. He looked exactly like that. I knew him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for your help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I'm sorry, I diverted my mind for a moment. Now this tape that has been played, that's not yet an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I would like to have it tendered into evidence. Actually, just this segment of the tape number V0001260, and the length of the segment is seven seconds. And you can see Slavko Dokmanovic giving an interview on this segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would propose that we receive the whole of the tape as marked for identification, Mr. Vasic. And we have the clip, the one still, as a photograph, as Exhibit 268. So marked for identification will be 269, the whole video. That should be enough for your purposes, should it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I respectfully inquire, while it's clearly a 65 ter document, what is the purpose of the document? I don't dispute the document, but is it being tendered to suggest that Dokmanovic was therefore not at Ovcara? My learned friend could perhaps clarify that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. With all due respect for my learned friend, I think that the purpose of this exhibit is to show that Dokmanovic, on the 20th of November, in this footage, was dressed differently than the description given by the witness of how he was dressed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there anything about date that's material to it, or place?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is the 20th of November, 1991. That's the date that the witness is talking about. The time is 1500 hours and 27 minutes on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the place?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The place is the centre of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, probably he returned from Ovcara and came to the centre, but I claimed that that was him. I identified Dokmanovic, but I did not identify the place where he was. I would like that to be recorded as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I am Borivoje Borovic, Defence counsel. You provided a large number of statements. You have already told my learned friend that, so if anything is in dispute, we can always check whether what I am presenting to you is correct. The Centre for Human Rights in Zagreb, you gave a statement and you confirmed that. My question is: Who did you give that statement to? Who questioned you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the medical centre for human rights. I'm talking about Ms. Kim Carter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You have to respond yourself. It was on the 18th of March, 1992, and it was the centre for human rights in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's how I wrote it down, then that's what it is. But I don't remember whether -- where that centre is in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you didn't give that statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not. It just means that I don't know where the centre is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in some centre, it doesn't matter now what it's called, you provided a statement in Zagreb that year, and do you remember who you gave the statement to?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a lot of statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably cannot remember all the places where I provided statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know who the barracks commander in Vukovar was when you were living in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see two -- two lieutenants when I was in Vukovar, but I don't know exactly who do you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you were at Ovcara, do you know who the commander of the Vukovar barracks was?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that no barracks commander from Vukovar mistreated you when you were at Ovcara? Is that what that means, since you don't know who it was?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the commander of the barracks was, perhaps I used to know that at one point, but please understand that this was a very difficult period. You had to accept or reject all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So do we agree that you don't know whether you were -- you don't know if were you beaten by the commander of the Vukovar barracks at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were shown a statement which is entitled, "What my experience of the fall of Vukovar is," "how I experienced the fall of Vukovar." You agree that you provided you that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I provided the statement to a journalist. I think I gave it to a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. You were also reminded of a note which you say you didn't sign. You said that you gave that statement, and in that note dated the 15th of May, 1992, drafted in the Vukovar police station, on page 1 of the B/C/S version, and also of the English version it says that as a sanitary inspector you went to inspect the kitchens in the Dunav Hotel and also in the city restaurant where food was prepared for the ZNGs and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said for the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was this in the Dunav Hotel and also in the city restaurant?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Dunav Hotel food was prepared for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And the city restaurant?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the soldiers, for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You would go to inspect the preparation of the food at the Dunav Hotel and in the city restaurant?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And in the Dunav Hotel, were there any people from outside of Vukovar there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. My learned friend, Mr. Vasic, asked you a little bit about that, about how the ZNG blockaded the barracks, that the barracks was surrendering, that they had even exhibited the white flag. You stated this in the Milosevic case on page 24537. You also said that an agreement was reached for the barracks to surrender, but an order had arrived from Belgrade that they shouldn't surrender. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were the stories going around in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain to us what was the reason for the surrender of the barracks and to whom was it supposed to surrender?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were probably aware that at the time a large number of barracks were surrendering en masse in Croatia from Varazdin all the way to the south. So it was logical for that particular barracks as the last one in Croatia to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And to whom was it supposed to surrender then?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Croatian army. To the citizens of the town of Vukovar and to the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In November 1991, was there a regular Croatian army or was this a paramilitary force called the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was called the National Guards Corps which then became the regular Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, that was always the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you officially.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which year. I don't know which year that was. Perhaps in 1962 or 1963, or perhaps at the time that I was in the detention camp or centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which year were you in the Detention Centre?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that you know that. It was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which month?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in November and then I left in January. So I came to Zagreb on my birthday, on the 5th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So it is your opinion that the Croatian army was established in 1963 or in late November or early December 1991? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case that was the Croatian army, regardless of its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And regardless of whether it was a regular army?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was regular, but it was a volunteer force as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Doesn't it sound a little bit illogical for you that a regular army would also be a volunteer army? In order for an entity to be regular in terms of military duty, then there is an obligation or a duty to be a member of that regular army and not to sign up on a volunteer basis?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all signed up voluntarily. Nobody ever in Vukovar was forced to join the Croatian army. I'm talking about Vukovar. I'm not talking about the whole of Croatia, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I think it is quite clear what you are asserting and what I am driving at. At the district court in Zagreb on the 26th of April, 2004 you gave a statement on the events of Vukovar, and you stated this yesterday. If you wish, I can show you this statement. On page 4 of the statement, paragraph 5, you said that the Croatian army comprised the following formations: Volunteers, MUP members, ZNG members, HOS members, civilian protection members, Croatian units, Croatian defenders, members of the HVO, but you think that there were very few of those, I think that that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what is strange about what I said?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Is everything that I read out to you and that you stated at the time correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In the Belgrade Ovcara case you stated that you were a retired officer of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but I resolved my status quite late.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What rank did you receive in the army?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So now you are a retired captain of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not a captain. I am not a captain, "kapetan," but I am a "satnik." Can you please tell me the difference? One is an apple and the other is an apple.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So you gave me an integral answer in the Serbo-Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can take it however you like. We understand each other well, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You responded to my learned friend Mr. Vasic's question that there were many volunteers from throughout Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a relative term. There were volunteers from many parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know from which towns they came? Would you be kind enough to repeat those towns?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came from Zagreb, Sisak, Slavonski Brod, Varazdin, Cakovec. Those were mostly -- that's where most of the men that I communicated or had contacts with came from. Maybe there were some other places too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know in which period they arrived at Vukovar, because you were in Vukovar throughout that whole period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dear, sir, if I were to write a diary, then I could reply precisely to each of your questions. However, I didn't keep a diary and none of my co-fighters kept one. Perhaps some did keep some records, but the things you are asking me about are difficult, so I have to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it like this, Mr. Cakalic: When was the first time that you saw volunteers from outside of Vukovar arriving at Vukovar? What month was it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say that -- well, I can't tell you exactly, but it was probably already September. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One of those, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Obviously not being a B/C/S speaker, one waits for the translation, but the nature of the cross-examination is the witness is not being allowed to complete his answers, and there is a dialogue going on which does not allow for correct interpretation or indeed the witness to have a chance to answer. I merely ask my learned friend to allow the witness to reply. I have no objection to him going along this line, but the witness must not be bullied in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think it's a matter of bullying at all, Mr. Moore. But I believe, Mr. Borovic, that your old enthusiasm is back, and if you could just hold yourself back until the witness is finished before you burst forth with the next question, it would make it easier for the witness, the interpreters, the transcript, and even for the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I entirely agree with your remark, Your Honour. This is not meant to bully the witness. It's my modus operandi which I shall try to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not afraid of you, if that's what you want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It appears that Mr. Moore is the only one who is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Interpretation remains a technical impossibility unless speakers are heard one at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have heard then what I was about to say. The importance is that the record reveals what it is that the two of you are discussing. And to get little bits of it is not enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In September, at least that's what you seem to believe, you said some volunteers started to arrive?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps even earlier, perhaps even earlier, I really can't say. I know they started coming but I can't say when exactly. It's asking too much even for me to specify the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the first time you saw volunteers arriving, who brought them there, how, and where exactly did they arrive? Is this something you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were arriving on buses or on foot wearing different kinds of uniforms, many with no uniform whatsoever, wearing their civilian clothes. I was wearing my civilian clothes all the time, just for you to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were most of them wearing military uniforms? If so, can you please describe them?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see what happened. When Dokmanovic was shown, he was in civilian clothes, but when he came to Ovcara he was wearing a military uniform. The soldiers arrived from Sisak were dressed like this, and those who from Zagreb were dressed like that. I can't give out statements like these. I myself didn't know for a long time who belonged to which unit and who came from where.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please be so kind as to describe some of the volunteers' uniforms, those who came to Vukovar. Can you tell us about that, please? I'm not asking about civilian clothes. I'm asking about some of the uniforms, some of the insignia. Did you see that at all?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the defenders, I think most of them were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the issue concerning the uniforms. I heard about the civilians. Can you remember any uniforms at all, any insignia that you saw the volunteers wearing?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about the insignia?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't say. I can't answer that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what type of weapons they had, they carried?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same type of weapons carried by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We spoke about water yesterday and water-related problems. My question is: You as a sanitation inspector, do you know about what sort of water was used for the barracks supplies? Was that from the city's water system?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no access there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their water came from the town's central water system, water-supply system. My inspection rounds did not include the barracks back in the former Yugoslavia. There was a special military team carrying out inspections there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you mention the barracks and about them wanting to surrender, where were the positions of the ZNG people in relation to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the barracks. Probably -- mind you, I'm saying probably. They were expecting something or there was an agreement for the barracks to surrender. Since a white flag had been hoisted, that probably was an indication of their intention to surrender. Now which parts of the Croatian army were there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about trying to remember where the military positions of the Croatian army were at the time in relation to the barracks. It was supposed to surrender to someone, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You didn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. There is a statement that we defined as -- that we defined as the statement with the following heading: "How I experienced the fall of Vukovar." You said on page 1, paragraph 3 of the English, page 1, paragraph 3 that on the 18th of November at about 2200 hours your wife and you left your building and headed towards the hospital. Further, you stated that those on duty did not allow you to enter the hospital. Would you please be so kind as to say who were these people on duty who refused to let you in? And who was standing at the hospital entrance at the time you came? Police officers or ZNG men?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I did eventually get into the hospital. I wasn't looking because the door was wide open. For the most part --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind, sir, I have to interrupt you. Is it true what I read from your statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I wrote that and signed that, then it must be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what the statement says, that some men who were on duty refused to allow you into the hospital. My question is perfectly simple. Who were these mean at the entrance who were checking who was coming in or leaving the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their names, but I know what I told them, to call Vukovic, Milicko.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who did you ask?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody who was there at the door, because you couldn't get further in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this person wearing a uniform? Was this person a police officer or a soldier of some kind?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that person was a soldier at all. I think it was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically. But then Milicko Vukovic came to get me and he was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to The Hague Prosecutors, page 4, paragraph 2, in English, page 4, paragraph 2, you stated you were already inside the hospital, and you described what's happening before you were about to leave. And you said: "I personally at the time did not see any other soldiers of the so-called JNA or Chetniks inside the hospital." Is it true that at the time there were no such persons there, the persons you described in this way?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement to the OTP, page 4, last paragraph, page 4, paragraph 5 in English, you stated in relation to what happened on the morning of the 20th of November, more specifically at 7.30 a.m. You said you saw two JNA soldiers who then frisked you or searched you outside, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said one of them was called Pero?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And the other was a Muslim, right? That's what your statement says.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how come you know this man called Pero? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person wearing JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit of a long story, really. They called us to -- they called on us to leave the hospital and to go to the courtyard outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to interrupt you, but this is all very nice and swell. However, we are running out of time. How come you know this man's name was Pero?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This soldier Pero was the one who drove us from Vukovar to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. How do you know that the other soldier was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably said so. I didn't make it up, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Next question: How do you know that they followed you all the way to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised them. I realised that those were the same men who rounded us up at the Vukovar Hospital and was the same two persons who drove us to Sremska Mitrovica. I know that for a fact. I even spoke to them along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Canadian investigators back in 1993 - on page 10, both English and B/C/S - you stated that you were mentally abused at the Vukovar barracks, but you referred to no physical abuse whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in relation to myself. But on my bus --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: There was no physical mistreatment, was there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not so sure about Samardzic. He might have been slapped once or twice. But I think only the soldiers were allowed on to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So is this portion of your statement correct, where you say that at the barracks you were, for the most part, mentally abused?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But not by the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My learned friend, Mr. Vasic, asked you several questions about this yesterday. I'll just expand on that a little. It's also in relation to the statement you gave. Page 45, page 44 and 45 of both the B/C/S version and the English statement. The investigator asked you whether there were any people on the buses wearing medical uniforms. And your answer was: "I advised many people back in the barracks to take those off. Some decided to listen to me, and those were the ones who fared better eventually." Today in reply to a question by Mr. Vasic, you said: "I told them to do that in order to protect themselves." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to explain to the Chamber why first of all you saw it fit to advise them; and secondly what you mean by protecting themselves?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If only they'd all listened to me. If only they'd all followed my advice. When we came to Ovcara there were three or four of them wearing white overcoats, medical uniform, the kind worn by doctors. You know what I mean. One of them was Veliki Bojler, Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said that yesterday; we know that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing that sort of uniform, and there were others who were. I tried to persuade them to take those off because they weren't who they were pretending to be. Those uniforms belonged to someone else, and they should put their own uniforms back on, otherwise something bad would happen to them, I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, sir, we can agree that those people on the buses who were wearing medical uniforms or overcoats, as you say, it makes no difference, that those people tried to pass themselves off as medical staff in order to avoid arrest or whatever it was that they were trying to escape from?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only they can tell. I didn't ask them. All I did was try to talk them into discarding those uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a considerable number of people wearing those uniforms on your bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Damjan Samardzic, I did see him. There may have been two or three other people, but I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you assembled outside the hospital, did you see a rather large number of people getting onto the buses wearing those white overcoats?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the people who were supposed to go to Ovcara together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday while testifying in chief you said that there were people on the buses. He asked what ethnicity and you said Croats, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a person there who was not a Croat, I now remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At this point in time -- you're still inside the hospital, before you get on those buses. Inside the hospital were most of people there Croats?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, sir, I didn't ask people about their ethnicity at the door or inside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Fair enough. Did you know all the people on your bus or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you then allow for the possibility that there may have been quite a number of Serbs on that bus unbeknownst to you, just because you didn't ask?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I there was one, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, how can a witness answer a question if he doesn't know who they are? He can only say the ethnicity surely of the people if he knows them. It's complete speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The effective evidence of the witness, Mr. Moore and Mr. Borovic, is that he knew -- identified people, he knew they were Croats, he did not know the other people, he did not know their ethnicity. I think that's where the witness is. That's the clear effect of the evidence. No further questions are needed on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I hope you won't hold this against me, but the Prosecutor asked yesterday -- I'll try to be as brief as possible. They asked who were the people getting on to those buses, and the witness said they were Croats. The general impression was that all the people who got on that bus were Croats. It's for the sake of this Chamber and for the sake of my own defence case that I'm trying to verify this fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now you've shown that it can't be proved by this witness. You've made your point, you've got there. So you have no need to go any further. He can only speak about the ethnicity of those he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This is a very specific question. Were all the people on that bus Croats or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a man named Kemal on my bus and he was not a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about all the others or the -- is it just that you don't know, as simple as that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I add something, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On another bus there was a man named Mitar Pucar, a Serb. He was not allowed to leave the hangar or taken outside, but rather was killed along with everybody else in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Cakalic, how long does it take to get from the centre of Vukovar to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I walked, it would take me about two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about if you drove?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 10 and 15 minutes. 15 tops.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said 10 minutes from the barracks, between 10 and 15 to reach Ovcara, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did say that, but why. When I went to Ovcara, I took the road to Belgrade, if you know what I mean. This was a different road, the road to Negoslavci, and that appears to be a shorter route to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a captain who searched you at Ovcara. You provided a detailed description of this. You said he had four stars on his epaulet and he had a large stomach, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was he a captain first class?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe he was a captain at all. He was just one of those people who put on an ill-fitting uniform and attached a random rank to his shoulder strap or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he did have the insignia corresponding to a captain, to the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Captain first class?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In the Ovcara case in Belgrade, page 33, and the English reference is 31, the date is the 25th of October, 2004. I'll just read this to you. The president of the Chamber asked you: "Were there people outside?" And he means outside the hangar because we're talking about the hangar now. Witness Cakalic: "Well, there were people. I don't know who they were." Presiding Judge: "No, no, it's fine. But now, according to your assessment, that's all I'm asking, according to your own assessment, how many people were there?"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: or nine or eight of them. I can't say. Anyway, it was around that number in the evening." And then the presiding judge asks a very direct question: "Could there have been over a hundred people maybe, 200, or perhaps 300?" Witness - that's you answering: "No, no." Is that true what you stated before the Belgrade chamber?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is still the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, there was the gauntlet. You've described that; I'm not going into that now. And in addition to that, there was a small number of people but not --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were turning around in a circle or, rather, rotating. Some were coming and some were leaving, but they were all coming there to watch us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But certainly not a number as great as the one specified by the presiding judge in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For as long as I was there, it was as I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you drawn breath, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to finish as quickly as possible, Your Honours, just to allow Mr. Lukic sufficient time. I have more questions, and you gave us three thirds of the entire time, and then I'll just pass the floor to Mr. Lukic, but I do have some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're going to have to break because of the tape, Mr. Borovic. And Mr. Lukic wants to get his breath back. So we will resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In your various statements you described your stay in Sremska Mitrovica. You said that, among other things, you were questioned on one day, on the 14th of December, 1991. And you were questioned by Goran Hadzic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And then the other person you said was called once Borivoje Jocic, and the other time you said it was Borivoje Savic. So is it Jocic or Savic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Savic. I have to clarify something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You registered some errors that I made, important ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, but you made very few mistakes. You seem to be -- to have good concentration.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you probably didn't read my statements carefully, because there is a major mistake that runs through all of my statements. And there is an error in four statements, and in the fifth statement that fact was stated correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in what capacity did Goran Hadzic question you on that occasion, and can you describe to the Trial Chamber who Goran Hadzic was at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic didn't interview or question only me in Sremska Mitrovica. He also interrogated some other citizens of Vukovar. For example, Ljubo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was interested in knowing the living conditions in Vukovar, and as regards my job, he was interested in that as well, and I told him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Were you also questioned by the colonel that we mentioned just a little bit ago?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was the commander of the camp. Yes. He did. Will you be putting some more questions? In that case, I will refrain from saying anything else other than that this colonel did interrogate me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Goran Hadzic, accompanied by Borivoje Savic, did he come during working days or did he come during the weekend or outside of business hours?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly on Saturday and Sunday when the JNA officers had days off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sremska Mitrovica is a town in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did this area also include Baranja, Western Srem and Backa or not?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the road to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did Goran Hadzic ever beat you while questioning you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He slapped me twice as I was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did a judge from Vukovar on any of those occasions attend these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He guarded the door. He was the judge of the Vukovar court and he stood by the door while Savic and Hadzic interrogated people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He died -- just give me a second to remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is it Branko Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Branko Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to us how come you were interrogated outside of business hours on weekends when there were no JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The judge did not interrogate me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. So what is your explanation? Why were they doing it only on non-business days? Were they doing something that was permitted or impermissible?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they either did something that was not permitted, or what they did was pursuant to an agreement with people in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You mean the jail officials?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean the officers who were there. You know that the Yugoslav army officers were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When asked by my learned friends that there was a Colonel Branko, do you think that there was an agreement with him?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never knew this colonel's name. He never introduced himself, but he did know my full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my cross-examination. Mr. Cakalic, I hope that you found this entire process to be decent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. And my suggestion to you is to look for the error that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That can be your homework, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I will raise this issue again. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Cakalic. And good afternoon to everybody else in the courtroom. Same to you, Mr. Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Novak Lukic. I am counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin, and I will putting questions to you now. We are always the last to cross-examine witnesses, and I seem to be in the habit of crossing out many questions put previously by my colleagues. I will try not to repeat any of the questions you heard earlier, and I will do my best to conclude this as soon as possible. Right at the outset I will ask our assistant to show you a short videotape. Please look at this video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Exhibit 118, which we saw in the courtroom previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cakalic, I will put three very simple questions to you and then afterwards we will revisit this event. First question: Have you ever seen this clip before?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I supposed. Can you tell me roughly how many times you saw it in your life?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only once?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him live only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm not talking about my client. I'm talking about this videoclip. My question is: How many times so far -- this seems to be a leading question indicating that you saw this a number of times. Can you tell us how many times you saw this altogether?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never counted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I suggest to you that this was shown on television at least every year on the anniversary of the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question relating to this video clip. Do you remember perhaps when you saw it for the first time? If you left prison in February of 1992, can you tell us if you saw that clip that year again, or for the first time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was in the sports hall for quite a long time. There was no television there. Then for a while I lived at Sljeme. I didn't watch television there either. Then I lived in Samobor, and I still didn't have television there. After Samobor I went to Jelsa, and I had a TV set there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some indication of what year it was?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Jelsa, it was 1960 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean ninety --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were quite active in your contacts with the commission for the missing persons and you attended negotiations in Budapest in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, when you were quite active and saw Mrs. Bosanac, Professor Hebrang and so on?
