utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see Professor Hebrang.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. In that period of time, after your release from captivity, did you see a photograph of my client somewhere?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many times. I saw his photograph many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that it dates back to Vukovar days?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those days and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I will go back to your testimony in chronological terms. I will be mostly interested in your stay at the hospital and also in some aspects of the barracks and Ovcara. You already said this to my colleagues, and I will cover this briefly. First you were a volunteer, if I may call it that, within the ZNG and later the Croatian army. We heard that later you were given a rank as well. Based on what I heard yesterday from you, it seems that you were also decorated -- no, that was the Red Cross. Were you ever decorated by Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I was able to see is that you never served a military service within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your previous answer was not recorded. You said that you were never decorated by Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I received nothing, not even a badge. I received a commendation from the association of camp-mates. Let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to your youth. I saw that you were exempted from serving in the JNA due to the fact that you had been wounded in World War II. You must have been a child there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that the reason that you were exempted from serving JNA ever?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please wait for me to conclude with my question before answering. You said that during the events in Vukovar you were in your house practically throughout the entire time until the 17th, or rather not in your house, in your apartment where you lived with your wife. You were there until the 17th of November and that sometime in the evening hours - you may have said at around 2200 hours - you decided to go to the hospital with your wife. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked at the Vukovar Hospital up until 1968; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came in 1960 -- I worked there for 10 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In one of your statements I saw that you worked at the hospital as the head of the medical laboratory and transfusion department from 1958 to 1968. I found this in one of your statements.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your wife was never employed at the Vukovar Medical Centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You covered this with my friend -- my learned friend Mr. Borovic, and we'll also interested in this. Based on what you said, I gather it wasn't easy to enter the hospital on the 17th in the evening and that via contacts with your friends with whom you used to work, you were able to enter the hospital and that after that you made it possible again through your contacts for your wife to enter the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was on the evening on the 17th, late evening, after 2200 hours. At that point in time in the late evening hours, were there any civilians in the hospital yard?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how many of them were there that evening in the hospital yard, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a figure. But there were many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you remained in the hospital on the 18th and the 19th, did you hear or did you see that in the course of these two days the civilians from the yard entered the hospital on the first floor? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They entered the hospital premises. I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to this large group of people. A figure of 1.000 or 1500 civilians were mentioned. Did they enter the hospital premises in those two days?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they did. Only those who had been at the hospital for a long time before that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will ask you this specifically. In the course of the following two days, if you ever left the X-ray department, did you see that there were a large number of civilians in the hospital yard?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went outside until we were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see -- did you hear from somebody who was with you in the X-ray department that civilians had entered the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I saw civilians once I entered the hospital -- or as I was entering the hospital. And I never left the X-ray department. So I'm not saying that there were many civilians there. Maybe somebody would have done it, but I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the point in time you arrived at the hospital, and you mentioned this yesterday to Mr. Moore, so perhaps you can clarify a little bit more, if you remember. In the course of that night from the 18th, 19th -- the 17th, the 18th and the 19th, did you hear any combat operations, shelling, shooting in the vicinity of the hospital? Do you recall anything like that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember hearing shooting. As I was going to the hospital, I did, yes. There was -- they were shooting when my wife and I were going there. It was the middle of the night. You could hear the -- the sounds of steps and somebody fired in our direction, not behind us, but in our direction, and I explained the circumstances in which we went to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the next few days, the 18th and the 19th, did you hear any combat operations during those nights?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were in a room, it was the dark room, so from there it was not possible to hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In response to questions you mentioned your pre-war activities in the headquarters of the Red Cross in Vukovar, and you mentioned Zeljka Zgonjanin?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if she made any lists of civilians, I'm talking about civilians, regarding the evacuation of Vukovar? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that she was very active in finding blood donors for all who came, even for one of your officers. He also received blood. Yes, she was making lists of people from Vukovar who were not only at the hospital but probably in other places. Excuse me, allow me just to finish my sentence. Since she was -- since the secretary of the Vukovar Red Cross fled without letting me know, I appointed Zeljka Zgonjanin town of Vukovar Red Cross secretary without consulting the assembly, because it wasn't possible to consult the assembly any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said during the examination-in-chief yesterday that you had an ID pass which was confiscated from you later at Velepromet and that you wanted to identify yourself using that so that you could take part in the negotiations. My question is: At the time you were in the hospital, did you know that negotiations were being conducted amongst the Zagreb side, the hospital and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were just children's tales. People were saying there will be boats or ships from Hungary and we will be taken to Hungary, or we will be allowed to go into unoccupied parts of Croatia. But all of these were just -- this was just speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you understood these just to be stories or tales?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understood them to be wishful thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear maybe that some sort of agreement was signed between Mr. Hebrang and General Raseta of the evacuation of the sick and the wounded?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that Mr. Raseta -- and I can't remember if he was a colonel or a general. Yes, he was a general. I heard that there was some negotiations. I don't know if the negotiations were conducted with Mr. Hebrang or someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All that I'm asking you is still while you were at the hospital. So during those couple of days when you were at the hospital, did you hear that lists where being compiled of the sick, wounded and the medical staff there? Did you hear of any lists being made at the departments?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first time I'm hearing it is now from you. Perhaps it did happen, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I just want to let you know that we heard testimony about that here already. You came to the hospital as a civilian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was always wearing civilian clothing. If I hadn't been wearing civilian clothing, I wouldn't be here with you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now with this answer you're telling me that I shouldn't put the next question to you, but I will put it to you anyway.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the JNA arrived on the 20th in the morning and when you were going towards the buses, did it occur to you to tell any of the JNA soldiers there that you were a member of the ZNG, that you were a volunteer who had taken part in some manner in the defence of the town? Did it occur to you to say that to anyone?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't crazy to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that on the 18th at Mitnica that Mitnica Battalion surrendered? In any case, that it was over 185 members of the ZNG, they said they were members of the ZNG, headed by Filip Karaula and they arrived at Sremska Mitrovica? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that when you were at the hospital at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So let's conclude the following on the bases of what you said. You came to the hospital as a civilian and you left the hospital as a civilian on the 20th when you were told to go to the buses?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole time I was in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like the usher to show the witness Exhibit 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will now see the floor-plan of the hospital, which we used during Dr. Njavro's testimony. To tell you the truth, this floor-plan is quite unclear to me. If the same is in your case, we will perhaps look at something else. Could you please show us where Marin Vidic was? Which room was Marin Vidic in? Now I'm talking about that time in the evening when you came. Perhaps we can turn the floor-plan. Mr. Cakalic, if this is too complicated for you, perhaps we'll try with a photograph, except I'm not sure that that can be seen on the photograph. But in any case, look at the floor-plan, and can you mark on the floor-plan the room where Marin Vidic was on the 19th in the evening? If it's too complicated, just please let us know.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't actually in that section of the building for a long time before that. The X-ray department was on the left side, and his office or room was entered directly. I remember entering it like that. We had a conversation before the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that room in the -- on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that the exit that was used when you were going out near the emergency department?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show the witness photograph 00531264? I think that's also an exhibit. The photograph of Vukovar Hospital. It's photograph number 9 from this set. No, not this one. This one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to see on this photograph Mr. Vidic's room, where Mr. Vidic was when Sljivancanin came? Can you see that room on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Surely the witness should be told that, since these photographs were taken in 1997, were they not, six years after the event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, lots of changes had happened since then. Thank you very much. It's like this: It's possible that the passage goes this way or that it goes that way. Vidic was in a room like this one, so directly when you enter the corridor, you go straight and then you would get to his room.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since it's quite clear to us in the courtroom where the plaster room is, was that other room close to the plaster room; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The X-ray was on the left side, that's where we were, and that room was further towards the middle or the central part of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue. Now I'm asking you about this encounter when Mr. Vidic was taken away. Yesterday during the questioning by the Prosecutor you said that this was when Sljivancanin came, sometime around midnight, between the 17th and the 18th.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, between the 18th and the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But in all your statements you say that this was the evening before the evacuation, so according to you am I right that it was actually on the night between the 19th and the 20th?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always confused those two dates, but I think it was on the night between the 18th and the 19th. I really couldn't swear by it, but I think that that was on the night between the 18th and the 19th. Others tried to convince me that it wasn't like that, that it was on the night of the 19th and the 20th, but it actually doesn't substantially change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, let's leave the dates aside. Was that the night before you were taken away, let's put it that way?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you personally see Sljivancanin come to see Marin Vidic? Where were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I happened to be in that very corridor. We had stepped aside a little bit not to be in the way. Mr. Sljivancanin came in his military uniform, dressed very nicely, the way he usually behaved, he was very charming, and he was accompanied by Bogdan Kuzmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You already said that.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to just put questions to you. I'm just interested in certain sections. I don't want to repeat myself. So you said that he came in the evening, it was quite late, sometime between 11.00 and 12.00?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was around midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You weren't able to hear their conversation. You stayed outside. After that they came out and Vidic was taken away. Was he taken away by Sljivancanin, did you see that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was walking either in front or behind. There was another person there, Bogdan Kuzmic. He was -- Sljivancanin was accompanied by Bogdan Kuzmic, so they took Marin Vidic. I didn't see him until Sremska Mitrovica, when I was delousing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before I continue with my question, I'm going to do something that the Prosecutor likes the best. I'm going to state my client's position. My client states, and in that sense I would like you to think before you give an answer. I know what you said during the examination-in-chief. So he claims that he came to the office of Marin Vidic sometime in the afternoon, at around 1600 hours, 1530 to 1600 hours. That at the time he was together with Nicholas Borsinger, that they were sitting together. Borsinger is a representative of the International Red Cross. They were sitting down and talking to Vidic and then that they left. And that Vidic was taken to Negoslavci at around 2000 hours. Before you give me an answer, I'm going to tell you two more things. That's why I would like you to think carefully. We have statements from certain Prosecution witnesses who are going to testify here, specifically captain first class who claims or asserts that at 2000 hours he escorted Vidic away. I'm going to tell you something else also.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be so. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But just one moment. I would like to say one more thing. I don't want to cause any confusion.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we already have a confusion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I am going to tell you one more thing, because it's not my goal to confuse you. I'm going to say one more thing. Mr. Vidic asserts that he was taken away at 2000 hours by this captain and not by Sljivancanin, because Sljivancanin had been to see him at around 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something that I don't know, who saw whom at what time, because we were not permitted to monitor that. All I know is that I remember when Major Sljivancanin entered Vidic's room, the major was accompanied by Bogdan Kuzmic. Bogdan remained outside in front of the door. I don't know what Sljivancanin talked about and how long they talked about, but he came out with Vidic, and Vidic was taken away. Now you say it was Negoslavci. I'm hearing of that for the first time, that he was taken to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that was late at night, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm saying that, just because Dr. Bosanac left the same night. And sometime in the morning at about 3.00 a.m., that's what I heard at least, she returned to the hospital. I think that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not trying to confuse you, so I will not be putting to you what Vesna Bosanac herself claims, but let's go back to something you said in answer to my learned friend from the OTP yesterday. Was he wearing a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sljivancanin. Moustache, at first you thought he was 180 centimetres tall, later you thought even taller, he was wearing a Tito cap. So these are the details that remain etched in your memory. And he was a major?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep saying was, was. I keep talking in the past. He was a major at the time. You can ask him if he really was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear at the time that he was a major? Did you see that he was a major? I'm talking about then, not what you saw later.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that he was a major by rank. He had a single star down the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While testifying in chief yesterday, you were asked if you had heard of him at the time, and you said on page 11 of yesterday's transcript that all of Vukovar had heard about him. That was my understanding at least. So you heard his name mentioned, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I'd seen him on TV too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Even before you saw him in person, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I saw him when he was standing outside the hospital, perhaps even -- he was stamping his foot on the ground saying, "This is Serbian soil, this is Serbian soil." Well, dear, sir, I have news for you. It's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he perhaps not saying, "This is my country, this is my country"?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am telling you is the way I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you saw that on TV just before you saw him in Marin Vidic, Bili's, office, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember that very clearly, you know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will go back to some of the statements that you made, only those you actually signed. [In English] Mr. Usher. [Interpretation] Let's briefly go back to one of your statements. I think that's the first one, VU hospital 46. I hope my learned friends have a copy of this statement in front of them. This is page 1; it's dated the 18th of March, 1992. You confirmed that you actually hand wrote this statement. I will be reading something on page 1, paragraph 3, it's the middle paragraph, last sentence: "In addition to this, I noticed a major enter Marin Vidic, Bili's, room and take him away. He was being escorted by Bogdan Kuzmic, who formerly used to work as porter at the hospital." You don't mention the name of my client here, although you knew of him at the time, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I can explain, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this is true. About half an hour or an hour before Marin Vidic was arrested, I was in his room. I asked him, "Marin, is there anything I can do for you?" And he said, "No, they'll be coming for me soon."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No doubt about that but I'm putting it to you that he was arrested at 8.00 and that he was arrested by Captain First Class Paunovic, that's my theory, and that Major Sljivancanin had been to see him at 1600 hours. All I'm asking you now is whether you mentioned his name in this statement or not, and you said you didn't. You have just confirmed that for me. His name is not mentioned anywhere in the statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose name?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you find that spot for me? Can you find that reference?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying it's not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, so then we agree. Let's move on in that case. What about that other statement, "How I experienced the fall of Vukovar." Page 2, please. Last paragraph. "After about 10 minutes I realised that a major entered his room who then took him away." Again, you failed to mention the name of that major, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please briefly go into -- or, rather, not go into private session and then I'll be asking you a question about this later on. At any rate, it is still your theory that the man who came and took Marin Vidic away was Veselin Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was on the 19th in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was at around midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to something else now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, you did not, I would submit, my learned friend unintentionally did not refer to the person who was accompanying the major. That is something certainly I don't have it on my transcript. If it's going to be put, and it's going to be suggested that there are inconsistencies, the Court have got to have an opportunity of checking whether those inconsistencies are correct. And there is reference to Kuzmic at that same time. Certainly in my English translation there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is beyond dispute that the witness does mention Kuzmic. What I have tried to show now is that in the statements he provided back in 1992 and later ones, we don't know the date of that other statement, but it's obviously after Vukovar. The witness never mentions my client by name. As for Kuzmic, I can hardly dispute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. But all I'm saying is, quite simply, if there is going to be an inconsistency suggestion, it has to be looked at in context. I accept entirely what my learned friend says, that Sljivancanin's name is not mentioned, but the text or the context has to be looked at, and there is reference to Kuzmic. My learned friend didn't read that out. That's all I'm objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Cakalic, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I didn't mention Major Sljivancanin's name, it was for a reason. I knew it full well that Vukovar would fall. We all did. And none of us wanted to mention anybody else. I think it should be easy for you to understand this. There were reasons for us doing so, and you have a thought and try to see if you can work out the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you go back to those two statements, just tell me yes or no, please. Do you mention any other JNA officers in those statements? Just if you do or if you don't. Don't mention their names, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I am saying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, no names. The question is: Did you mention any JNA officers there or not? No names, please?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I won't be pressing you on this. You stand by your previous statement that it was Sljivancanin. Another question in relation to my client's arrival when he came to Mr. Vidic's office. If, as you say, you saw him at the time, you said in a statement to the OTP, and you said yesterday you believed he was about 180 centimetres tall. My question to you now is without wishing to create further confusion, but is it possible that another officer with a moustache arrived at the time who was 180 centimetres tall and took Marin Vidic, Bili, away? Could you rule out that possibility?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I definitely rule out that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's all for this topic. Let's move on now to the next morning, the morning of the 20th. My learned friend Mr. Moore was quite quick when dealing with this yesterday. Do you remember whether in the morning of the 20th Dr. Matos appeared, telling you that all the civilians were to walk down the corridor and leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That had previously been ordered by Dr. Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see Dr. Bosanac in the corridor that morning?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So he just conveyed her words to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He and -- there was another man with him. I didn't know who that man was. It was said that all those who were inside the building and were not employees of the hospital should leave. And we complied.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard about you being searched outside the emergency ward. Many witnesses have testified to that. During the search, was Mr. Guncevic near you; if so, how far from you was he?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were outside the hospital, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was on the bus. How far, I don't know. They were cursing us, cursing our mothers and our fathers, those two soldiers who were given the task of getting us all in a line and taking us away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But during the frisking itself, you don't know how far from you he was standing at this in time point?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He may have been standing next to me, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not pressing the point at all. But do you remember that as you were being searched you were also searched for sharp implements but none of your personal belongings were taken away? I mean money, documents, watches, that sort of thing? The searching in the corridor outside.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a man called Pero. There was another one -- there was another man with him whose name I don't remember. All the dangerous implements in our pockets were to be pulled out and placed on the ground in front of us. And we obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your money wasn't taken, your documents weren't taken from you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those things weren't taken away. At least my weren't. But I think the same applies to all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you now please have a look at your statement to the OTP? This is page 6. The English reference is page 4. Page 6, last paragraph. Would you please just follow, sir?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- wooden club, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, page 6. Do you have the statement you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "How I experienced the fall of Vukovar," this is mine. 537459.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a different copy of the statement, but I'm sure we can find our way around this. The passage, the paragraph begins with: "At 9.30 or 10.00 a.m." It should be page 4 or page 5. We obviously have different copies of the same statement.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we're talking about 537463, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I gave you a copy that's marked differently from mine, but it's the same statement. The paragraph begins with the following words: "At 9.30 or 10.00 a.m." This is page 6 in my copy. It's about what's going on at the hospital before you leave and go to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll read the next paragraph to you, it says that: "At 9.30 or 10.00 a.m." -- I'll read it slowly. "At 9.30 or 10.00 a.m. those two soldiers told us to get on the buses parked outside the auxiliary entrance to the hospital on Gunduliceva Street. When I reached the place where the buses were parked, I saw five buses, and we were told to get on the buses. There was no special system to decide who would be getting on which bus. As soon as one bus was full, they would send people on to the next bus. And no records were kept as to who was getting on the buses." Did I read this correctly?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by this, because you haven't actually testified to this now?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by it. What I wrote here is my account of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on, please. You testified in chief yesterday mentioning a number of names of people who you remembered were with you on the bus, Berghofer, Guncevic, Damjan Samardzic. First of all, do you know a man called Professor Licina, and do you remember if this man was on your bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him as being on my bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that case we might as well move on. What about the name of Rudolf Vilhelm? Does that ring a bell? Was he on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. He was a tall lad. I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where exactly you were seated inside the bus? Maybe I'm asking too much. Was it down the middle of the bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably towards the rear of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Left or right, because there are seats on either side of the bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what did you have for lunch on that particular date? Yes, I was seated on that bus and I was seated on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There you go. You probably know why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will be pursuing that through my next questions. Very well. A couple more questions relating to the situation before you left. Can you give us the approximate time when you all got on to the bus and before the buses left from Gunduliceva, how long did you spend in the bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was approximately at 8.00 in the morning, but don't take my word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just interested in the time-frame, approximately.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it was about an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that hour did anybody enter the bus; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the hospital.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anybody leave the bus?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some people whose wives worked at the hospital left the bus. I think that was the question. I don't know the names of all the people, but I don't think you can ask me for that anyway. But anyway, a number of men or several men went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you assert that Major Sljivancanin got on the bus, said if there were any people there that had any connection with hospital staff, and then those few people left the bus with him. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that it was him?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you, we heard a lot of testimony here that a lieutenant did enter the bus, but that it wasn't my client, that's why I'm asking you. Are you sure that it was him? You didn't say that any time before, so that's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether it was him or somebody else, I don't know. I couldn't really be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm even more happy with the answer if you are not sure. Very well. Now I'm going to move to the part about when you set off for the barracks. You described these events yesterday, you described an event that I heard about for the first time yesterday. In no statement did you describe a situation that you were crossing a bridge and that you could see another bridge. What I understood was that you said that you were going past the old pastry shop?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Capiks [phoen] pastry shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, so I understood you properly, but the English interpretation was incorrect. Then you said that you saw a man standing there who you thought was Vance but then it turned out not to be Vance, and then there was Sljivancanin there, according to you, and they were there -- or he was there as you were crossing the bridge. Will you agree with me that the fact that you saw Sljivancanin there at that place you did not mention in any previous statement?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I spent all night going through it and checking.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we ask the registry to show us a photograph. That is photograph marked 00531236. It's exhibit number that I already provided earlier to the registrar. I don't have it written here with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you will see a photograph. I think it's Exhibit 256. Do you see the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do we see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Then we will be more specific. Can you see the bridge which you took across the river when you were going from the hospital to the barracks, or shall we zoom in a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it's okay. I can see that bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to zoom in a little bit on the middle part of the photograph. Excellent. Could the usher please go to the witness. If you can, can you mark your movement on the photograph, the direction that the bus moved in across the bridge, and can you mark the place from the bridge where you saw my client?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the bridge. Are you following?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you indicate the direction of your movement with an arrow, please, if you can?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And next to that can you place the number 1?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now can you mark on the photograph where you saw -- where you saw that scene that you saw from the bridge?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This high-rise building, actually, is in the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you like us to zoom in a little bit?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that we will then have to take a different photograph.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we can tender this photograph into evidence first, and then if we manage to zoom in, then we can see what the witness can do, and we can use this one to show the direction in which his bus was moving. We could tender that as the first piece of evidence because then I am afraid we will not be able to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can it being clear what is the precise place that is marked? Is it the tip of the arrow? Or a dot or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I would like to try to find out from the witness is the place where he saw allegedly my client. What he indicated now is the direction in which his bus was moving as he was going from the hospital to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he marked that with a number one?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to zoom in more with this photograph, but since he's already marked it, I wanted to tender this into evidence first, and then we can go back to the next step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit number 270, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I marked is the bridge along which we were moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you can just wait a little bit and then we will zoom in a little more on that section of the photograph. Can you see that area now where you saw my client with the man who you thought was Cyrus Vance?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were moving along the right bridge. We were moving along the right bridge, and here, near the Njegica house, I saw at a slant --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that with a pen? Mark the right bridge which you were moving along on which you were moving with an arrow, and now where did you see my client?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this on the bridge itself or somewhere next to the bridge?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was maybe a little bit more to the right, but that's where I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you mark with the number 1 the direction in which you were moving, and with number 2, the place where you saw Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us approximately how far apart these two bridges were?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 50 metres, perhaps. Maybe less.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time you still had the glasses that were later broken?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of the prescription strength that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this photograph into evidence now, because we don't want to lose the marking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 271.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. I have a couple of more questions on this topic, but perhaps we could go on a break now, Your Honours. I don't know if we're approaching the time for the break? No? All right then, we will just continue. If it's still not time, then I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We could take the break now, or you could have about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer to take the break now, Your Honours, because I wanted to refer to some text later, so I would prefer that to be in one piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you allow me just to deal with two very short matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The first relates to the following witness. Mr. Smith, as you can see, is here and ready to proceed, and the witness is outside court. We've spoken to Mr. Lukic. I think he has said that he will take the rest of the day, there or thereabouts. From what I can understand, this is his indication. I have a small amount of re-examination, and I therefore anticipate that we will not get on to the next witness. Might I ask that that witness be released? If not, then the witness can remain and we can start as and when Your Honour wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been dreadfully bad at assessing how long I will take. All I can say is that I am two-thirds through my cross-examination. There is one-third of my questions to go. I'm not sure how much time that will take. But I think at least 30 minutes, up to 40 minutes. My self-assessment is horribly poor. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we will assist you. What about 20 minutes then, Mr. Lukic? In view of that, and in view of Mr. Moore's anticipation of some re-examination, we might have at the best perhaps quarter of an hour, perhaps nothing, for the next witness. In those circumstances, we again could say that the next witness will not be called before tomorrow. But that brings me to a contingency, which is besetting us at the moment. We were listed tomorrow for a late start at 3.45 because of a decision being given in another case. We've been informed during this last break that the decision in that other case will take longer, and, in fact, could go well until 5.00. The trial presently being conducted in Courtroom II, which is the only other courtroom, may, by 7.00 tonight reach the position where a witness is finished, in which event they will not have a witness tomorrow, in which event we could use Courtroom II and we could start at 2.15, which, I think, would be desirable, if there is no problem with any counsel. But we won't know that until the end of the sitting in the other court tonight. So I cannot give your next witness and Mr. Moore any confident statement about when we will be able to reach the next witness. The worst scenario is that we would have only one session late tomorrow in this courtroom. But I would hope it will be possible to start earlier than that. If not at 2.15, at least at sometime before 5.00 in Courtroom II. I'm sorry, but as we are reduced to two courtrooms, we have these constant pressures. So subject to the contingency of an unknown starting time tomorrow afternoon, the witness need not remain tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour probably saw I was trying to indicate to Mr. Lukic one other matter. We had, the Defence and myself, or the Prosecution, had decided to have a meeting tomorrow through that period, trying to resolve difficulties in relation to agreed facts. The agreed facts are 98 per cent done, quite simply. There are other matters that we were just going to try and fine-tune, but if needs be, we can bring that back in time sometime tomorrow morning. It's rather difficult just to say exactly where we stand, whether we should bring that meeting back or whether we should keep it where it was at about 2.15, and then as soon as the Court is ready to resume, we can come straight in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, I would suggest keep it where it is to minimise disruption. If it becomes clear by 7.00 that we can start at 2.15, you would be invited then to arrange an earlier time, if you could, for your meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly. Thank you very much. May I just deal with a second matter? It's -- it's simply this: The witness sometimes comes into court, this witness perhaps because of Your Honour's requirements and the present scenario, and is often in court for 10 or five minutes sitting by himself. I know that the witness service finds that the witnesses themselves find it an unpleasant experience; they feel very isolated. I wonder if it's possible for a witness to come in after the Bench has come in? I know that occurs in other Trial Chambers, and that way then they don't have to sit and listen to conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is possible. It would lose a little more time. I am conscious that just at the moment our resumption times tend to be delayed simply because there are so many other pressing matters filling every moment of the break and they are unpredictable. We can try and make some administration arrangement to ensure a witness doesn't come in unduly before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it may be that on occasions we can leave it that they come in after us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that courtesy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, when should I start my clock running on the 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll see how fast registrar is able to help me. I would like to bring back that photograph showing the bridges and show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One thing I would like to ask you firstly, could you please repeat the name of the pastry shop; it wasn't recorded. And if you could please mark its spot on the photograph, just those two things.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pastry shop owner is called Djordje Njegic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that street or square?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the new name is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the old name?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to live on that street a while ago. But I can't remember. Look, that wasn't my last address. That was the first address I had when I first arrived in Vukovar, when I came to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you could just mark the location of that pastry shop in this photograph for us, please.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I seek that this be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 272.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You needn't look at the photograph now. You testified yesterday that you saw outside that shop a man who you believed at the time to be Cyrus Vance, right?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you find out that this man was not Cyrus Vance, that you mistook a different person for him?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once photographs were shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was then that I established that this person was not Cyrus Vance but a different person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you try to be more specific? Which year was that? From 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day I was taken to the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was in Vukovar while all of this was still going on?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after the fall as we were being taken to the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was as early as that that you knew for a fact that that man was not Cyrus Vance, the man you had seen?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now read to you a portion of your testimony in the Belgrade trial dated the 25th of October, 2004. For the benefit of my learned friends from the OTP, the English reference is 10, page 10. The Prosecutor will be making sure if my reading is accurate, so I don't need to show you the transcript, just to speed things along a little. Your words, sir, on that page: "At that point in time when Marin Vidic, Bili, was arrested, Mr. Vance was nearby. At this time I thought to myself, Well, we will probably not come to any grief because one of the greatest peacekeepers in all of Europe is here. However, I think he was in the company of Mr. Carrington. I can't swear, though, but based on a photograph that I saw, I think that it was Mr. Carrington. I did see Mr. Vance." In Belgrade in 2004 you were still positive that you saw Cyrus Vance in Vukovar at the time. That was back then. And yet now you are telling us that it was as early as 1991 that you understood that that person was not Cyrus Vance. Which is true?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's how memory plays tricks on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You testified in Belgrade under oath; you are now testifying here under oath. This detail may strike you as unimportant, but it certainly matters to me. It matters to the overall picture. Did you not state in Belgrade that you had seen Cyrus Vance in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. I read the statement myself. However, I did some soul-searching afterwards, and I realised that that person was not Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yesterday while testifying in chief you said you were not certain whether you saw any military officers standing next to Mr. Sljivancanin and that man?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did see Mr. Sljivancanin on the bridge, near the edge of the bridge, right next to the pastry shop you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at that statement with the heading "How I experienced the fall of Vukovar." Page 3. The ERN is 00593578.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is page 3. I'm reading the last paragraph. And I'll read a portion in relation to the barracks, because that's what we're moving on to next. "We are crossing the bridge, and on the adjacent bridge I see people in white watching the ruins of the town."

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's your statement "How I experienced the fall of Vukovar." 03571625, that's the page number down at the bottom. The last paragraph. I'm reading the second sentence of that paragraph to you the last paragraph: "We are crossing the bridge," can you see that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "down Gunduliceva Street."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll read on from there. "We are crossing the bridge, and on the adjacent bridge I see people in white watching the ruins of the town. They are bringing us to the barracks. We are entering the compound, the buses, one by one, about 30 to 40 metres. Once we stop, some Chetniks approach us and several soldiers wearing olive-drab uniform. The bus on which I was was next to the hangar where the ammunition was kept. Chetniks start approaching the buses and then the mental abuse begins." Did I read it accurately?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll move on to the barracks, but there is another thing in relation to the our previous subject. In this statement you only mention seeing people in white on the adjacent bridge, but no reference there to my client, is there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And the reason I'm saying this is because my view was -- you see, this is the bridge. Can you see that? Do you have the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't, unfortunately. But please describe that for us because we still remember the area.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's the pastry shop there, and then there's the bannister of the bridge, and then the trees that you can see in the photograph, they were standing right there. My view was to the left, and I could actually see that from the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. There is another thing --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I have something to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When were these photographs taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose the OTP could tell you, but I assume they were taken in 1997, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly. Can you see these trees between this building and the River Vuka. I think the trees, too, were destroyed by shells. And that may be why I was better able to get a clear view.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just another question for me to assess your powers of perception. You said that the distance between these two bridges may be about 50 metres. My question: You see the high-rise building right there, how high do you think it is?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's probably seven or eight floors, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How high could that be?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, say, one floor is about 280 centimetres or 300 centimetres, so there you have it. You just add it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. We no longer require this photograph. What I've read to you now nearly concerns the barracks. Based on the statements that I have shown you and what you told my learned friend Mr. Borovic today, those people mentally abused you, mistreated you. You defined those people as Chetniks or reservists?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I came across the concept of reservists in one of your statements, so that's why I'm saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a couple of questions in relation to Ovcara now, if we can please go into private session. I will be mentioning persons whose names should not be uttered in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are now to move to the other facilities. I must admit that your movements between Ovcara, Velepromet and the barracks is a bit unclear -- are a bit unclear to me and I wanted to clarify. Yesterday you stated that as far as you can remember you spent two days at Modateks. Do you still agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came in the evening. I said that we were not taken in at Velepromet and that we were taken to Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat all that. Yesterday you said that you spent two nights at Modateks. Are you certain of that?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been three, even.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from Modateks and the barracks, do you know the date at which you arrived in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I probably forgot it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case --

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we spent some time in Sid for about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is of no importance to me.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What matters to me is the date, if you can remember it.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the part you were explaining is what we've had already heard. From Modateks you were taken to Velepromet to the death room and the carpentry shop, as you explained. Can you remember what time of day or night it was when you left Modateks for Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was still daylight, it was during the day. There was a man who came to used to work at the bank; he was at the back. And another one we used to call Dedica [phoen] was in the front. They took us to Velepromet to the death room and they left us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you explained that some people there told you something along the lines, "Let us have Berghofer" and this and that person. Where were they in relation to the room of death? Were they inside the Velepromet compound or outside?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Let us have Berghofer, let us have Cakalic." I remember the incident but not the exact place where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But those were people who knew you?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I recall. Thank you for reminding. They were outside the compound on the right side of the road, and we were entering the compound on the left side, depending on where one stands. We came from the direction of Modateks, and they were on our right-hand side. Had we come from Vukovar, they would have been to our left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In response to Mr. Moore's questions regarding the room of death and the two guards, you said that those were young soldiers wearing the typical JNA uniforms, and you weren't able to say whether these were regular soldiers or not. But I wanted to ask you the following: Were they wearing the same uniform as the person you mentioned who was just outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And approximately of his age?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. They were his peers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may have a moment. Yesterday you stated that Perkovic, Karlo Crk, Martin Sajtovic were killed at Velepromet. What I gathered from your testimony is that they were taken outside of that room and that you never saw them again?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's how I put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I needed to ask you this to make my conclusions. So you never saw anyone killing them?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them being killed, but I heard that somebody was killing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on the sounds you heard?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that they were killing people there?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it may be of importance for this Tribunal. Did you hear that from anyone? If not, we may just continue.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard later that they were killed and buried. But not at Velepromet. That's not where I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether their bodies were ever found?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read somewhere or I may have been told by someone that Karlo Crk's body was eventually found in a village in the direction of Tovarnik and then to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were told this by someone?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that his body was found there in the place where Croatians were tied up and then shot at. But I believe you're familiar with what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After Velepromet you were transferred to the barracks; you described that. And yesterday during your testimony you said that at the barracks you saw the beating, once you were taken in, fed and given cigarettes, that some people came in and administered beatings. My question, hence, is whether the beatings took place in the room where you were?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the very room where you were?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are about to conclude, but I wanted to clarify one last thing. I'm interested in whether you could offer a comment. This is a document, and I would kindly ask the registry to show the witness a document bearing the number 2D 050018. These are the lists provided by the OTP, the lists of detainees at Sremska Mitrovica, and not all of the lists were admitted, and I believe the OTP was to do that at a later stage. I just wanted to get a comment from this witness. Could we please zoom in at number 206? Mr. Cakalic, I can read the following data here: Your name and last name, I believe the next name is your father's name, as well as your date of birth, the 5th of January, 1934. What follows is what we use to call the individual number of a citizen, and the date of capture. We see here the 19th of November, 1991. Hence, my question: Once you left the camp, and I believe the date is mentioned here as well, could we please go to the right a bit further? The 7th of February, 1992, that's the date of your release?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the 19th of November is what is confusing me. My question is whether you provided this data to the Croatian authorities when you were arrested, so to say, or was this introduced by someone else based on some other information?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The date of your capture is the 19th of November, 1991. And I believe that was not the date when you were taken away.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm confused with this date. Who provided this information?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been me. I told you already that I keep mixing those two dates, the 19th and the 20th, even as we speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have this admitted as evidence, although I believe this is a voluminous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 273.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to say one thing. I came from captivity on my birthday. And that was my true birthday, when I came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have just three topics. Let's deal with your glasses. You have told us about the prescription that you had, but let's forget about the prescription for a moment. Were you long-sighted, short-sighted? How was your sight in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991 they broke my glasses. I talked about that incident. It was that soldier wearing captain's rank uniform, but I knew that that didn't really fit him. That's when he took my glasses and he broke them. He tried them on himself, they didn't fit, and then he threw them down and stepped on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. But I'm talking about your glasses being broken, and what we want to know is without your glasses what could you see? Were you able to read or were you able to see long distances? Can you tell us once your glasses were broken whether you were long-sighted and short-sighted? We need to know. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's clear to me. I was far-sighted. Even now I am far-sighted, but close up, then I have to read like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on to the second topic. You were shown a video with Mr. Dokmanovic. Do you remember seeing that, about two hours ago, although it may seem much longer?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just put our minds back, please, to November 1991. How well did you know Mr. Dokmanovic at that time? How long had you known him?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him at least six or seven years before that. He was a foreman at a plant. It was in the direction of Osijek, the turning to Bobota. He was a foreman at an agricultural plant. I don't remember the name. It was the Bobota agricultural farm, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's clearly the way I've asked the question. You see, what's been suggested, probably, is that Mr. Dokmanovic was not at Ovcara and you didn't recognise him correctly. Now, do you follow? So the Court needs to know how well you knew Mr. Dokmanovic, and how reliable that identification is. Do you follow? So can you tell us how well you knew Mr. Dokmanovic before the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him many times, I would go to Bobota -- actually to Trpinja. He's from Trpinja. I knew his father and I knew him too. I'm sure, I'm convinced, I could swear it was Dokmanovic. Not just me, all the others said that also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were asked by Mr. Borovic, the gentleman with -- to your left, I won't describe him. You were asked about the dress at Ovcara, the way people were dressed. Now, you were asked about volunteers, and this was the question, so please listen as carefully as you can to it. I know it's been a long day: "Can you be so kind as to describe some of the volunteers' uniforms, those who came to Vukovar?" All right? Now, when we refer to "volunteers," we're referring to volunteers on behalf of the JNA Serbian side. That's the way the word "volunteers" is being used there. Now, you made the following reply --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I am objecting because the context of "volunteers" was actually in the context of Croatian army volunteers, the defenders of Vukovar, so I think that would have been the correct context by the Prosecution. At that point in time "volunteers," in terms of Serbian volunteers, were not discussed. I think the witness can also confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well that's exactly the reason I'm asking the question, because the witness says: "As for the defenders," and there is a distinction being drawn by the witness between defenders and volunteers, so I am asking the witness to clarify whom he means by volunteers, whom he means by defenders. I can read out the context if my learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's fine. The way you were posing the question wasn't putting it that way. If you adjust your question, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The defenders of Vukovar, the Croatian defenders of Vukovar, the ones who went to Ovcara, what way were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all wore civilian clothing. They had their own clothes. I don't think that anyone came in any kind of particular uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you, then, about what I will call Serbian or JNA volunteers or paramilitaries that you saw at Ovcara. Can you tell us how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Some were wearing civilian clothing, some had mixed clothing. They wore uniform tops and just regular bottoms. For some it was the other way around. These were paramilitary units at Vukovar and men that I knew. For example, one of them came to me when we were already out of the hangar, and he asked me, "Uncle Emil, what are you doing here?" So I said, "What am I doing here, what everyone else here is doing." This was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, just to focus on the uniforms now. Can you please continue with your description of the way the Serbian paramilitaries or paramilitaries were dressed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was obviously thinking for too long. I should have objected earlier. I think putting the question in this way, in the re-examination, arising from the cross-examination, is a very broad interpretation of topics that can be dealt with in re-examination. The Prosecutor now is initiating a topic that was not a topic initiated during cross-examination. The topic was something that had to do with the uniforms or clothing worn by the defenders of Vukovar. The Prosecutor now is asking some question that is too broad. This is maybe something that he failed to question the witness about, and now he's trying to put the question to the witness, but it wasn't a topic put to the witness during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It was a topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, my recollection of the cross-examination, not of you, is that there were questions which went to the capacity of this witness to recognise the various uniforms and to identify them. And I think it gives rise properly to an attempt to clarify just what is the extent of this witness's knowledge of that matter. Please continue, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I've virtually finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal, please, with the paramilitaries and the uniforms that you have described? What other uniforms did you see at the Ovcara hangar?

utterances.speaker: EMIL CAKALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Zoric, who saved me and who was killed in a traffic accident in Vukovar, which I am very sorry about because I would like to pay him back for what he did, he was only wearing a jacket of the JNA and a Tito cap, as well as a white ribbon, based on which I assume that he belonged to the White Eagles. Others belonging to the Territorial Defence, others that I saw there, Dr. Ivankovic's son had a cockade. He had a Chetnik hat with a cockade on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no additional re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. You will be pleased to know, Mr. Cakalic, that that brings to an end the questions that we have for you. We thank you for your attendance, your patient attention to the questions, and for the assistance you've been able to give us. And you are, of course, now free to return to your home. If there is no other matter -- could I mention that we have been told, unfortunately, that the trial in Trial Chamber II is now continuing tomorrow, and inevitably, therefore, we are faced with a start at 1645 at the earliest. It may be a little later than that, depending on how long the decision takes in the other case. Is there any concern that that is an inadequate time for us to make use tomorrow? It does give us a full session, save an hour and a half sitting. And I think we could use that time usefully, unless there are significant concerns. Very well. We will adjourn to tomorrow, it appears it will be in this courtroom. It cannot be between -- be before 4.45, and it will be then or as soon after that as we are able to regain possession of the courtroom. Thank you again, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of March, 2006, at 4.45 p.m.

--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.54 p.m.,
